sentence: How ___ sugar do you take in your coffee?
explanation: 'Much' is used with uncountable nouns like sugar; 'many' is for countable plurals.

sentence: How ___ people came to the meeting?
explanation: 'Many' is used with countable plural nouns like people; 'much' is for uncountables.

sentence: We haven't received ___ information about the delay.
explanation: 'Information' is uncountable, so 'much' is required in the negative sentence.

sentence: There are too ___ tourists in Venice in August.
explanation: 'Too many' is used before countable plurals like tourists; 'too much' is for uncountables.

sentence: How ___ luggage are you taking?
explanation: 'Luggage' is an uncountable noun, so 'how much' is used.

sentence: There weren't ___ chairs, so some guests had to stand.
explanation: 'Chairs' is countable and plural, so 'many' fits; 'much' and 'little' are for uncountables.

sentence: Does the project need ___ more work?
explanation: 'Work' is uncountable here, so 'much more work' is correct; 'many more work' is impossible.

sentence: How ___ eggs do we need for the cake?
explanation: 'Eggs' is countable and plural, so 'how many' is used.

sentence: There is so ___ crime in this area that people are afraid.
explanation: 'So much' is used with uncountable nouns like crime; 'plenty' would need 'of'.

sentence: Not ___ candidates applied for the position.
explanation: 'Not many' is used with countable plurals like candidates; 'not much' is for uncountables.

sentence: There's ___ milk left — just enough for one cup.
hint: positive meaning: a small amount is enough; 'milk' is uncountable
explanation: 'A little' means a small but sufficient amount and is used with uncountables like milk.

sentence: We had very ___ rain this spring, so the garden suffered.
explanation: 'Little' means not much and is used with uncountables; the garden suffering shows an insufficient amount.

sentence: Only ___ people attended the talk, which was disappointing.
hint: countable plural; 'only a few' is the natural pattern
explanation: 'Only a few people' is the standard way to say a small number; 'only few' is not used.

sentence: He's lucky: he has ___ good friends he can rely on.
hint: positive meaning with a countable plural
explanation: 'A few' means some — a positive idea — and is used with countable plurals like friends.

sentence: Very ___ applicants had the required experience.
hint: 'very' + negative quantifier with a countable plural
explanation: 'Very few' means almost none and is used with countables; 'very a few' is impossible.

sentence: I'd like ___ more time to think about your offer.
explanation: 'A little more time' means a small additional amount; 'time' is uncountable so 'a few' is wrong.

sentence: The village is remote and has ___ facilities — not even a post office.
hint: negative meaning with a countable plural
explanation: 'Few facilities' means almost none, which matches 'not even a post office'; 'facilities' is countable.

sentence: Don't worry, we still have ___ time before the gates close.
hint: positive meaning: there is some time; 'time' is uncountable
explanation: 'A little time' means some time, which reassures; 'time' is uncountable.

sentence: She made very ___ mistakes in the essay, so she nearly got full marks.
explanation: 'Very few mistakes' means almost none, which explains the high mark; 'mistakes' is countable.

sentence: Can I ask you ___ questions about your trip?
hint: polite request with a countable plural
explanation: 'A few questions' means some questions and is the natural pattern in polite requests.

sentence: There's ___ point in complaining — no one will listen.
hint: fixed expression: ___ point in doing something
explanation: 'There's little point in doing something' means it is hardly worth doing; 'point' is uncountable here.

sentence: He took ___ notice of the warning and carried on as before.
explanation: 'Take little notice of' means to pay hardly any attention; 'notice' is uncountable here.

sentence: Would you like ___ more tea?
explanation: 'Some' is used in offers and requests where we expect agreement; 'any' is for neutral questions.

sentence: I haven't got ___ cash on me — I'll pay by card.
explanation: 'Any' is the normal quantifier in negative sentences; 'haven't got no cash' would be a double negative.

sentence: ___ of my friends knew about the concert, so I went on my own.
explanation: 'None of my friends' means zero friends; 'no' cannot stand before 'of' and 'nothing' is not a quantifier here.

sentence: There's ___ at the door — go and see who it is.
explanation: 'Somebody' is used in affirmative sentences for an unknown person; 'anybody' belongs to questions and negatives.

sentence: I looked everywhere, but I couldn't find my keys ___.
explanation: After a negative verb, 'anywhere' is used; 'somewhere' belongs to affirmative sentences.

sentence: I asked ___ in the office, but nobody knew the answer.
explanation: 'I asked everybody' (all the people) contrasts with 'nobody knew'; 'everything' refers to things, not people.

sentence: We went to the exhibition, but there was ___ worth seeing.
explanation: 'But' introduces a contrast, so 'nothing worth seeing' fits the disappointment.

sentence: She's very fussy — she refuses to eat ___ green.
hint: after 'refuse' the clause is negative in meaning
explanation: Verbs like refuse, deny and avoid create a negative context, so 'anything' is used.

sentence: The hall was so crowded that ___ found a seat.
hint: a crowded hall means no one succeeded
explanation: 'So crowded that nobody found a seat' matches the logic of the sentence; 'anybody' cannot be the subject of an affirmative clause.

sentence: ___ smells burnt in here — can you check the oven?
hint: affirmative statement about an unknown thing
explanation: 'Something' is used in affirmative sentences for an unknown thing; the request to check the oven shows the speaker believes it.

sentence: Have we got ___ eggs for breakfast?
explanation: 'Any' is the normal quantifier in neutral questions; 'none' cannot stand before a noun.

sentence: I'd love ___ help with the decorating, if you're free.
explanation: 'Some' is used in requests and hopes where the speaker wants agreement.

sentence: There is ___ milk in the fridge — help yourself.
hint: affirmative statement; the invitation confirms it
explanation: 'Some milk' fits the affirmative statement and the invitation; 'no milk' would contradict 'help yourself'.

sentence: It's so quiet here — there's hardly ___ around.
explanation: 'Hardly' is a negative adverb, so it combines with 'anybody' (hardly anybody = almost nobody); 'nobody' would double the negative.

sentence: He had ___ money, so he couldn't even buy a bus ticket.
explanation: 'Had no money' states zero and explains the result; 'none' cannot stand directly before a noun.

sentence: We need to find ___ who can fix the boiler.
hint: affirmative statement: an unknown but existing person
explanation: 'Someone' is used in affirmative sentences; 'anyone' belongs to questions and negatives.

sentence: Let's find ___ quiet to study.
explanation: 'Somewhere' is used in affirmative sentences; adjectives like 'quiet' follow the -where word.

sentence: The box was empty — there was ___ inside.
explanation: 'Empty' explains 'there was nothing inside'; the other options contradict emptiness.

sentence: Don't rush — we've got ___ of time.
hint: fixed pattern: ___ of time (no article needed)
explanation: 'Plenty of time' needs no article; 'lot of time' would need 'a', and 'much of time' needs 'the'.

sentence: There's ___ of room for improvement in this essay.
explanation: 'Plenty of room' is the fixed pattern; 'a lot of' would need the article 'a', which is not in the sentence.

sentence: He made a ___ of money in property.
hint: the article 'a' is already in the sentence
explanation: 'A lot of money' is the fixed phrase; 'a lots of', 'a plenty of' and 'a deal of' do not exist.

sentence: We had a ___ of fun at the fair.
explanation: 'A lot of fun' is the fixed phrase; 'fun' is uncountable and the article 'a' forces 'lot'.

sentence: There are plenty ___ chairs for everyone.
hint: 'plenty' is always followed by this preposition before a noun
explanation: 'Plenty of + noun' is the fixed pattern; no other preposition follows 'plenty'.

sentence: A ___ of people complained about the noise.
hint: the article 'A' is already in the sentence
explanation: 'A lot of people' is the fixed phrase; 'a lots of' and 'a plenty of' are wrong, and 'a great' needs 'deal ... of'.

sentence: It cost a great ___ of money to repair the roof.
explanation: 'A great deal of' is used with uncountable nouns like money; 'a great lot of' and 'a great plenty of' do not exist.

sentence: There were ___ people in the lift, and it broke down.
explanation: 'Too many' is used before countable plurals like people; 'too much' is for uncountables.

sentence: I put ___ sugar in your tea by mistake.
explanation: 'Too much' is used before uncountable nouns like sugar; 'too sugar' is impossible.

sentence: This suitcase is ___ heavy to carry.
hint: adjective + this word + to-infinitive = impossible result
explanation: 'Too heavy to carry' means it is more heavy than possible; 'very' and 'so' cannot be followed directly by 'to'.

sentence: He isn't old ___ to drive a car.
explanation: 'Old enough' means sufficiently old; 'enough' follows the adjective, while 'too' gives the opposite meaning.

sentence: We haven't got ___ chairs for everyone.
explanation: 'Enough chairs' means a sufficient number; 'too' before the noun would give the wrong meaning and position.

sentence: You've given me far ___ information.
explanation: 'Far too much information' is the correct intensifier pattern; 'far much' and 'far very' do not exist.

sentence: It's ___ cold to swim today.
explanation: 'Too cold to swim' means the temperature prevents swimming; 'enough' would follow the adjective.

sentence: Is it warm ___ to swim?
explanation: 'Warm enough' means sufficiently warm; 'enough' follows the adjective.

sentence: He was driving ___ fast for the icy road.
explanation: 'Too fast for something' means faster than is safe; 'so fast' needs a 'that' clause, not 'for'.

sentence: There isn't ___ room in here for a piano.
explanation: 'Enough room' means sufficient space; the negative 'isn't' shows the space is insufficient.

sentence: ___ of the students has been given a personal timetable.
hint: this is the only option that can be followed by 'of' and take a singular verb
explanation: 'Each of the students has ...' is correct; 'every' cannot take 'of' here and 'all/both' need a plural verb.

sentence: ___ everyone in the office passed the safety test.
hint: the only adverb that can modify 'everyone'
explanation: 'Almost everyone' is the standard pattern; 'each', 'all' and 'every' cannot directly precede 'everyone'.

sentence: She carried a suitcase in ___ hand.
explanation: 'Each hand' views the two hands individually; 'every hand' is not used for body parts this way.

sentence: The night bus runs ___ twenty minutes.
explanation: 'Every twenty minutes' expresses regular intervals; 'each twenty minutes' is not used.

sentence: ___ time I visit Rome, I discover something new.
explanation: 'Every time I ...' introduces repeated occasions; 'all time' and 'whole time' are not used here.

sentence: ___ of her two brothers lives abroad.
explanation: 'Each of her two brothers lives ...' is correct; 'every' cannot take 'of' and 'both/all' need a plural verb.

sentence: The tickets cost fifteen pounds ___.
hint: price per item comes at the end
explanation: 'Fifteen pounds each' means fifteen pounds per ticket; 'every' cannot stand alone in this position.

sentence: ___ single room in the hotel was fully booked.
explanation: 'Every single room' is the emphatic collocation meaning 'without exception'.

sentence: She gave the children two sweets ___.
hint: distribution per child at the end of the sentence
explanation: 'Two sweets each' means two per child; 'every' cannot stand alone here.

sentence: We see our grandparents ___ other weekend.
explanation: 'Every other weekend' means alternate weekends; 'each other' has a different, reciprocal meaning.

sentence: ___ of my parents is retired.
explanation: 'Neither of my parents is ...' is correct for two items with a singular verb; 'both/all' need a plural verb and 'none' is not used for two.

sentence: There are two cafes here, but ___ of them is open on Mondays.
explanation: 'Neither of them is open' is correct for two items with a singular verb; 'both' and 'all' would need 'are'.

sentence: You can park on ___ side of the street.
hint: singular noun meaning 'this one or that one'
explanation: 'Either side' means one side or the other (both are allowed); 'both' would need the plural 'sides'.

sentence: ___ of the two films has been shown on television.
explanation: 'Neither of the two films has ...' is correct for two items; 'none' is not used for two and 'both/all' need a plural verb.

sentence: She speaks ___ Spanish and Italian fluently.
explanation: 'Both ... and ...' links two items affirmatively; 'neither/either' pair with 'nor/or'.

sentence: ___ the food was eaten within minutes.
explanation: 'All the food' is correct with an uncountable noun; 'whole' needs 'the whole of' and 'both' needs two separate items.

sentence: We had five applications, but ___ of the candidates was suitable.
hint: more than two candidates + singular verb
explanation: 'None of the candidates was ...' is used for three or more; 'neither' is reserved for two.

sentence: We can take the ferry or the tunnel — ___ way takes about three hours.
hint: one of two options, singular noun
explanation: 'Either way' means whichever of the two you choose; 'both' would need 'ways'.

sentence: ___ John and his brother are doctors.
explanation: 'Both John and his brother are ...' links two people affirmatively; 'neither' and 'either' pair with 'nor/or'.

sentence: He has lived in Berlin and Prague, and loves ___ cities.
explanation: 'Both cities' refers to the two cities mentioned; 'all' would suggest three or more.

sentence: There are trees on ___ side of the road.
hint: singular noun: each of the two sides
explanation: 'Either side' means each of the two sides; 'both' would need the plural 'sides'.

sentence: ___ of my two brothers work in banking.
explanation: 'Both of my two brothers work ...' is correct; 'all' and 'none' are not used for two.

sentence: I don't like ___ of these two paintings.
explanation: After 'don't like', 'either' is used: 'not ... either of them' means zero of the two; 'neither' would double the negative.

sentence: We inspected the four bridges, but ___ of them was safe.
explanation: 'None of them was ...' is used for three or more items; 'neither' is only for two.

sentence: The twins are ___ over six feet tall.
explanation: 'Both' is used for exactly two; 'all' is for three or more.

sentence: ___ the information you gave was correct.
explanation: 'All the information' is correct; 'none/neither' would need 'of' and 'both' requires two separate countable items.

sentence: This cup is cracked — could I have ___ one?
explanation: 'Another one' means one more, unspecified; 'the other one' would mean a specific second cup.

sentence: Some people like classical music, while ___ prefer jazz.
explanation: The pattern 'some ... others ...' contrasts unspecified groups; 'the others' would need a previously defined group.

sentence: She has two children. One lives in Leeds, and ___ lives in York.
hint: one of a pair of two
explanation: 'One ... the other ...' is the pattern for exactly two; 'another' would imply more than two.

sentence: I'll see you ___ day.
hint: an unspecified day in the future
explanation: 'Another day' means some other, unspecified day; 'the other day' refers to the recent past.

sentence: Where are the ___ guests? Haven't they arrived yet?
explanation: 'The other guests' uses 'other' as an adjective; 'others' is a pronoun and cannot precede the noun.

sentence: Three of the six books were mine; ___ were my sister's.
hint: the defined remainder of a set of six
explanation: 'The others' refers to the specific remaining books in the known set of six.

sentence: The hotel was full, so we had to look for ___ hotel.
explanation: 'Another hotel' means some other, unspecified one; 'the other hotel' would imply exactly two known hotels.

sentence: One of my shoes is tighter than ___.
hint: shoes come in pairs of two
explanation: 'One ... than the other' is the pattern for two items; 'another' would suggest more than two.

sentence: Some metals are magnetic; ___ are not.
explanation: 'Some ... others ...' contrasts unspecified groups; 'the others' would need a closed, known set.

sentence: I don't like this colour — do you have it in ___ colours?
explanation: 'Other colours' uses 'other' as an adjective before the plural noun; 'another' is followed by singular nouns.

sentence: ___ words, the plan is too expensive.
explanation: 'In other words' is the fixed phrase for rephrasing; 'another' cannot modify the plural 'words'.

sentence: Five students passed. ___ all failed.
hint: the defined remainder of a known group
explanation: 'The others' refers to the specific remaining students; 'the other' is singular.

sentence: This year the festival attracted ___ visitors than in 2024.
explanation: 'Fewer' is the comparative for countable plurals like visitors; 'less' is for uncountables.

sentence: Try to eat ___ sugar and more vegetables.
explanation: 'Less' is the comparative for uncountable nouns like sugar; 'fewer' is for countables.

sentence: The new model has ___ moving parts, so it breaks down less often.
explanation: 'Fewer moving parts' is correct because 'parts' is countable and plural.

sentence: If you walk instead of driving, you'll spend ___ on petrol.
explanation: 'Spend less' is the comparative with uncountable money; 'fewer' is for countable nouns.

sentence: She spent a great ___ of time preparing the report.
hint: fixed phrase: a great ___ of + uncountable
explanation: 'A great deal of time' is used with uncountable nouns; 'a great number of' needs a countable plural.

sentence: A large ___ of students have applied this year.
explanation: 'A large number of students' is used with countable plurals; 'amount' is for uncountables.

sentence: A ___ of people object to the plans.
explanation: 'A large number of people' is correct for countables; 'a great deal of people' and 'an amount of people' are wrong.

sentence: It took a great ___ of courage to admit the mistake.
explanation: 'A great deal of courage' is the standard pattern with uncountables; 'a great number of' needs countables.

sentence: Three out of four respondents — that is, the ___ — supported the change.
hint: three out of four = more than half
explanation: Three out of four is more than half, so 'the majority' is the correct label.

sentence: The ___ of teenagers own a smartphone these days.
explanation: 'The majority of + plural noun' means most of them; 'the number of teenagers own' would be ungrammatical.

sentence: ___ people enjoy a sunny holiday.
hint: general statement without 'the' — 'people' has no article
explanation: 'Most people' means people in general; 'most of' needs 'the' (most of the people).

sentence: ___ the students passed with good grades.
explanation: Before 'the + noun' use 'most of': 'Most of the students'; 'most the students' is wrong.

sentence: This is ___ beautiful beach on the island.
explanation: 'The most beautiful' is the superlative form used for comparisons within a group.

sentence: She was ___ in a bad mood.
explanation: 'Mostly' is an adverb meaning mainly or usually; 'most' as a quantifier needs a noun.

sentence: ___ of what he says is nonsense.
explanation: 'Most of what he says' is the pattern 'most of + noun clause'; 'the most of' is wrong.

sentence: ___ lakes in this region freeze in winter.
explanation: 'Most lakes' speaks about lakes in general; 'most of' would need 'the lakes'.

sentence: ___ of the workforce is part-time now.
hint: pattern: ___ of + specific group; singular verb
explanation: 'Half of the workforce is ...' is the correct pattern; 'the half of' is not used in this position.

sentence: Cut the orange in ___.
explanation: 'Cut something in half' is the fixed expression; 'in middle' would need 'the middle'.

sentence: ___ attempts were made to contact her.
explanation: 'Several' is used with countable plurals; 'much', 'little' and 'a great deal of' need uncountables.

sentence: He faced ___ charges of fraud.
explanation: 'Several charges' means more than two; the other options are used only with uncountable nouns.

sentence: ___ of the milk has gone off, so do not drink it.
explanation: 'All of the milk' — 'whole' would need 'the whole of the milk'.

sentence: There's ___ point asking him again — he never replies.
explanation: 'There's no point' — 'point' needs the adjective 'no', not the pronoun 'none'.

sentence: We had ___ luggage that the taxi couldn't take it all.
explanation: 'So much luggage that …' — luggage is uncountable.

sentence: ___ students joined the trip this year than last.
explanation: 'Fewer … than' for countable students.

sentence: She has ___ patience with rude customers.
explanation: 'Little patience' — uncountable and insufficient.

sentence: There were ___ than twenty people at the meeting.
explanation: 'Fewer than twenty' — countable people.

sentence: ___ candidate was given five minutes to speak.
hint: one at a time, singular verb
explanation: 'Each candidate was given' — singular agreement; 'all candidate' is wrong.

sentence: Hardly ___ came to the afternoon lecture.
explanation: 'Hardly anyone' is already negative — do not add 'no one'.

sentence: There isn't ___ room for another desk in here.
explanation: 'Not enough room' = insufficient space.

sentence: ___ of the two proposals has been approved so far.
explanation: 'Neither of the two' — 'none' is for three or more.

sentence: ___ money was spent on advertising last year.
explanation: 'Little money' — uncountable noun.

sentence: There is ___ use asking him — he never checks his messages.
explanation: 'There is no use doing something' = it is pointless.

sentence: ___ of the three routes avoids the toll entirely.
hint: not any of three or more
explanation: 'None of' is used for three or more; 'neither' only for two.

sentence: We have made ___ progress than we hoped by this stage.
explanation: 'Progress' is uncountable, so the comparative is 'less'.

sentence: There were ___ interruptions this year, so the ceremony ran far more smoothly.
explanation: 'Interruptions' is countable plural: fewer.

sentence: There was ___ enthusiasm for the proposal, so it was quietly shelved.
explanation: 'Little' (without 'a') means not enough — which explains shelving the proposal.

sentence: ___ the rooms in the hotel have a sea view; the rest face the car park.
explanation: Before 'the rooms' a partitive is needed: Some of; 'all/none' contradict the context.

sentence: ___ of the equipment has been serviced this year, so breakdowns are rare.
explanation: 'Most of + noun' = the majority of it; 'the most' is a superlative.

sentence: Hardly ___ of the villagers had ever seen a passport.
explanation: 'Hardly any of' = almost none of; 'hardly none' is impossible.

sentence: The lecture was ___ attended than the organisers had hoped.
explanation: 'Well attended' compares with the adverb: less well attended.

sentence: There are ___ than forty applicants for every training place.
explanation: 'More than' + number expresses quantities above a figure.

sentence: She has ___ patience with excuses; deliver on time or do not bother coming.
explanation: 'Has no patience with' — 'no' directly negates the noun.

sentence: Every one of the switches ___ been tested twice.
explanation: 'Every one of' takes a singular verb: has.
